newsitem.title: UK: POLL-EU issue a turnoff for UK voters-Reuters/NOP.
newsitem.headline: POLL-EU issue a turnoff for UK voters-Reuters/NOP.

text.p: An election debate over Britain's links with the rest of Europe has left voters cold, a Reuters/NOP opinion poll showed on Wednesday.

In a survey of 1,093 people around Britain conducted on Tuesday, 53 percent said the question of Britain's role in Europe would not at all affect the way they intend voting in the election on Thursday.

The poll, carried out in 52 parliamentary constituencies, gave the opposition Labour party a 22 percentage point lead over the 18-year old Conservative government, according to NOP's adjusted results.

Some 22 percent of those polled said the Europe debate, currently at the heart of Conservative party divisions and at times a heated issue in Britain's marathon election campaign, had not affected their voting intentions very much.
Only 10 percent of respondents said the European issue was a big factor in their decision.
Experts say, apart from Europe never having been an issue to fire voters' imagination, apathy towards the European issue was due to pragmatism.
If plans to implement a single European currency had been more advanced, it would have become a more emotive issue with a bigger impact on voting intentions, analysts said.

"(Europe) is not the thing that is most important to them. They are more concerned with domestic issues, such as health and education, where they feel they can make a difference," said Neil Carter, lecturer in politics at the University of York.
"There is little difference because both parties have promised a referendum on the single currency."

Voters found little to distinguish between the two main parties on Europe. Thirty-three percent said they most trusted Labour to represent the country's interests in Europe and 29 percent the Conservatives. Nine percent said they would trust the Liberal Democrats, the poll showed.
Asked what kind of ties with Europe would be better for Britain's economy, regardless of the political advantages and disadvantages, 35 percent opted for the status quo.

"People don't want more integration until they know what it entails," said John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester. "There are no clearly defined positions and the debate has been further confused by the Conservatives' squabbling over the issue."
Twenty-five percent said the economy would benefit from closer links with Europe while 27 percent preferred a looser association.
Relations with Europe took centre stage in the campaign a week ago with Major and Blair trading jibes over who would best represent Britain in negotiations towards a single currency.

Blair's party was infuriated with the Conservatives when the ruling party placed an advertisement in national newspapers showing the Labour leader sitting as a puppet on the knee of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Major has portrayed himself as the only leader able to take a tough stance on European integration with Britain's EU partners
